title: The Medieval West
subtitle: From the reforming monks to the eve of Wittenberg. Papal power at its height, the cathedrals and the universities, the crusades and the inquisition, and the long refusal of reform that made Luther possible.

sections.title: Two False Stories
sections.body:
There are two easy ways to tell the story of the medieval church, and both are false. The first is the old Protestant polemic, a thousand years of darkness between the apostles and Luther, nothing but superstition and corrupt priests. The second is the romantic picture, an age of faith when Europe was whole and everyone believed and the world still sang. Neither survives the evidence. The centuries between the break with the East and the eve of Wittenberg were the church's noon and the church's sickness at once, and those were not two stories. They were one.

Consider what this church actually was. It baptized every child, married every couple, buried every body, and stood at the center of every village in Europe. It ran the schools, fed the poor, kept the calendar, sheltered the traveler, and held nearly all the learning that had survived the fall of Rome. A person could live an entire life without one significant day the church did not touch. No institution in Western history has held that kind of place before or since, and none is likely to again.

And the same church, holding all of that, preached armed pilgrimages that ended in massacre, built courts that used torture, taxed the forgiveness of sins, and burned the men who said so out loud. We will not choose between these facts, because history does not let us. The task is to hold them together, and to remember the whole time that the church which did both is the church we come from. Its height and its corruption are not someone else's inheritance. They are ours.

sections.title: The Monks Who Cleaned the Church
sections.body:
The reform began at the edge, not the center. In 910 a duke in Burgundy founded a monastery at Cluny with one unusual provision. No king, lord, or local bishop would control it. It answered to Rome alone, and in practice to its own abbots and its Rule. That independence mattered because the church of that age was owned. Nobles installed their relatives as bishops. Kings handed churchmen the symbols of their office. Priesthoods were bought and sold openly, a trade the church called simony after the magician in Acts who tried to purchase the power of the Spirit. Cluny modeled a church governed by its calling rather than its patrons, and within two centuries hundreds of monasteries had taken up its pattern.

Then the reforming spirit did something remarkable. It captured the papacy itself. Gregory the Seventh, the fiercest of the reforming popes, took office in 1073 and declared war on simony and on the royal appointment of bishops. When the German king Henry the Fourth defied him, Gregory excommunicated him and released his subjects from their oaths, and in January of 1077 the most powerful ruler in Europe stood for three days as a penitent in the winter cold outside the castle gate at Canossa, waiting for a monk to absolve him. Gregory himself died in exile a few years later, remembered as saying that he had loved justice and hated iniquity and therefore died in exile.

A compromise on appointments came at Worms in 1122, but mark what had happened. The reform had freed the church from the grip of kings. It had also taught the church to stand above them. Both lessons took, and only one of them was safe.

sections.title: Christendom at High Noon
sections.body:
By the thirteenth century the Western church stood at an altitude no church has reached before or since. Innocent the Third, pope from 1198 to 1216, placed whole kingdoms under interdict and watched their kings yield. England's King John surrendered his realm to the papacy and received it back as a vassal. In 1215 Innocent gathered the Fourth Lateran Council, which defined the doctrine of the Mass, required every Christian to confess and commune at least once a year, and legislated for Europe like the parliament of a single Christian civilization. That is what Christendom meant. Not a religion inside a society. A society inside a religion.

And the age built things that still stand. The great Gothic cathedrals rose across France and England in these centuries, stone lifted toward heaven by towns that could barely feed themselves, and they can still make a modern visitor go quiet. The cathedral schools at Bologna, Paris, and Oxford grew into the first universities, with theology at the head of the curriculum. Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican friar teaching at Paris, built his vast Summa on the conviction that faith and reason are friends, and his death in 1274 left it unfinished and unmatched.

The same era produced a different greatness. Francis of Assisi, a rich merchant's son, stripped himself of everything around 1209 to live with the poor and the lepers, and Dominic founded an order of preachers to teach a faith everyone was assumed to hold already. The friars were a living question posed to a wealthy church. It says something good about that church that it made room for them. It would not always.

sections.title: What the Power Did
sections.body:
Now the other ledger, and we will not soften it. In 1095 Pope Urban the Second summoned the knights of Europe to recover Jerusalem, and the response outran anything he imagined. Before the armies left, crusading bands massacred the Jewish communities of the Rhineland at Worms and Mainz in 1096. When Jerusalem fell in 1099, the crusaders slaughtered its people, Muslim and Jew alike. In 1204 a crusade turned aside and sacked Christian Constantinople. In 1209 the church launched a crusade against heretics in the south of France, and at Beziers the army killed the town without sorting believer from heretic.

The instruments grew more systematic. From 1231 the papacy commissioned inquisitors to hunt heresy, and in 1252 a papal decree authorized torture in the church's own courts. The same council that ordered yearly confession also ordered Jews to wear distinguishing dress. None of this comes from the church's enemies. It is all in the records the church kept about itself.

How did the people of a crucified Lord come to this? Not, for the most part, through cynicism. Through certainty joined to power. These men believed souls hung on conformity, and they held the sword, and that combination did what it always does. This is the part of the story where a modern believer wants to look away or explain, and we should do neither. We are not better than they were. We are Christians who have rarely held that kind of power, which is a different thing, and the record suggests it is the power, not the century, that corrupts.

sections.title: Babylon and the Broken Papacy
sections.body:
The height did not hold. In 1302 Pope Boniface the Eighth issued the most sweeping claim of papal authority ever written, declaring that submission to the Roman pontiff was necessary to the salvation of every human creature. Within a year, agents of the French king had seized and humiliated him at Anagni, and he died weeks after. The message was brutal and plain. Kings no longer stood barefoot at Canossa. By 1309 the papacy itself had moved to Avignon, in the shadow of the French crown, and there it stayed for nearly seventy years, while critics compared the era to Israel's captivity in Babylon.

Catherine of Siena, a dyer's daughter with no office and no army, wrote letter after letter to Gregory the Eleventh and finally went to Avignon in person to tell him to go home to Rome. He went, in 1377, and then it got worse. The election of 1378 split. Rival popes reigned at Rome and at Avignon, each excommunicating the other's obedience, while the kingdoms of Europe chose sides by politics. A council at Pisa tried to end the scandal in 1409 and managed instead to produce a third pope. There were saints praying on both sides of the line, which tells you how deep the confusion ran.

The Council of Constance finally ended the schism in 1417 with a single pope. The same council had already taken Jan Hus, a Czech preacher who came under an imperial promise of safe conduct to plead for reform, and burned him at the stake in 1415. It condemned the dead John Wycliffe too, and his bones were later dug up and burned. The institution had healed itself. It had also shown what it did to the men who told it the truth.

sections.title: What Made Luther Possible
sections.body:
So we reach the question this era leaves us. Why did the Reformation come in 1517 and not sooner? Not for lack of reformers. The medieval church grew them in every century. Cluny reformed the monasteries, Gregory reformed the papacy, Francis and Dominic reformed the streets. Waldo of Lyon preached apostolic poverty around 1180 and was condemned for it. Wycliffe was condemned. Hus was burned. Savonarola, who called Florence to repentance, was hanged and burned in 1498. The councils that tried to set the whole church's authority above the pope's were outmaneuvered within a generation. Reform kept arriving, and the structure kept absorbing it, or killing it.

Meanwhile the structure rotted. The Renaissance papacy produced popes with mistresses and acknowledged children, a pope who led armies in his own armor, and a court whose luxury scandalized the pilgrims who saw it. The theology of indulgences, stretched in 1476 to cover souls in purgatory, matured into a fundraising machine, and in the 1510s that machine was set to work rebuilding Saint Peter's in Rome. Erasmus mocked it all in print and stayed in the old church anyway, and a joke of the age said that Erasmus laid the egg Luther hatched. Under everything sat the press. After Gutenberg, around 1450, the next Hus could not be silenced by burning one man. His words could outrun the fire.

The verdict is not that the medieval church lacked faith. It is that the church so fully identified its structures with the gospel that it treated its physicians as enemies. That disease is not medieval. Every church that confuses its own power with Christ's kingdom catches it, ours included. In 1517 the bill came due.

keyFigures.name: Gregory the Seventh
keyFigures.note: The reforming pope who brought King Henry the Fourth to Canossa and died in exile.

keyFigures.name: Innocent the Third
keyFigures.note: Pope at the summit of papal power, who made kings yield and called the Fourth Lateran Council.

keyFigures.name: Thomas Aquinas
keyFigures.note: Dominican friar whose unfinished Summa argued that faith and reason are friends.

keyFigures.name: Francis of Assisi
keyFigures.note: The merchant's son who chose poverty and reproached a wealthy church by his life.

keyFigures.name: Catherine of Siena
keyFigures.note: The dyer's daughter whose letters helped bring the papacy home from Avignon.

keyFigures.name: Jan Hus
keyFigures.note: Czech reformer burned at Constance in 1415 under a promise of safe conduct.

keyFigures.name: John Wycliffe
keyFigures.note: Oxford scholar who attacked church wealth and inspired the English Bible, condemned after his death.
